prompt: What causes day and night on Earth?

options.text: The Earth spinning on its axis
The Earth orbiting the Sun
The Sun moving around the Earth
The Moon blocking the Sun at night

feedback.b: One orbit of the Sun takes a whole year, not a day.
feedback.c: The Sun only *seems* to move across the sky. It's the Earth that is turning.
feedback.d: The Moon is often in the daytime sky, and it doesn't block the Sun every night.

hints: How long does it take to go from one sunrise to the next?
solution: The Earth **spins on its axis** once about every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day, and the side facing away has night.

prompt: About how many days does it take the Earth to orbit the Sun once?
hints: It's the length of one year.
solution: One orbit takes about **365¼ days**, which is one year. The extra quarter day adds up to a whole day every four years, which is why we have leap years.

prompt: Put the planets in order, starting with the one **closest** to the Sun.
hints: A memory trick: **M**y **V**ery **E**ager **M**other **J**ust **S**erved **U**s **N**achos.
solution: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The first four are small rocky planets; the last four are giants.

prompt: What is the Māori name for the cluster of stars whose rising before dawn in midwinter marks the Māori New Year for many iwi?
hints: It is known internationally as the Pleiades.
solution: **Matariki**, known internationally as the Pleiades. Its reappearance in the dawn sky in midwinter marks the start of the Māori New Year for many iwi.

prompt: Match each word to its meaning.

right.text: The curved path of one object around another in space
The imaginary line that the Earth spins around
A natural object that orbits a planet
A large, round object that orbits the Sun
When one object blocks sunlight from reaching another

hints: The Earth spins on its axis and travels around the Sun in its orbit.
solution: Orbit: the path around another object. Axis: the line the Earth spins around. Moon: orbits a planet. Planet: a large, round object orbiting the Sun. Eclipse: one object blocking sunlight from another.

prompt: What causes the seasons on Earth?

options.text: The tilt of Earth's axis as the Earth orbits the Sun
The Earth being closer to the Sun in summer
The Sun giving out more heat at some times of the year
The Moon's position in its orbit

feedback.b: A very common idea, but wrong. Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, which is winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
feedback.c: The Sun's output stays almost the same all year.
feedback.d: The Moon affects tides, not seasons.

hints: If distance caused the seasons, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time. Do they?
solution: Earth's axis is **tilted** (about 23.5°). When our hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, the Sun is higher, its light is more concentrated and days are longer, so it's summer. When we're tilted away, it's winter.

prompt: After a new moon, the lit part of the Moon gets bigger each night. We say the Moon is [[a]]. After a full moon, the lit part gets smaller, and we say the Moon is [[b]].
hints: To 'wax' means to grow.
solution: Growing is **waxing**; shrinking is **waning**.

prompt: What is the name of the unit equal to the average distance from the Earth to the Sun (about 150 million km)?
hints: Jupiter is about 5.2 of these units from the Sun.
solution: The **astronomical unit (AU)**. Jupiter, for example, is about 5.2 AU from the Sun.

prompt: Which of these orbit the **Sun** directly (not a planet)? Select **all** that apply.

options.text: Mars
Pluto
An asteroid in the asteroid belt
A comet
The Moon
Titan, a moon of Saturn

hints: Moons orbit planets.
solution: **Mars** (a planet), **Pluto** (a dwarf planet), **asteroids** and **comets** all orbit the Sun. The Moon orbits the Earth, and Titan orbits Saturn.

prompt: What is a **light-year**?

options.text: The distance light travels in one year
The time it takes light to reach Earth from the Sun
A year on a planet that gets a lot of sunlight
The time light takes to travel 1 AU

feedback.b: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. A light-year is a distance, not a time.
feedback.c: It has nothing to do with years on other planets.
feedback.d: That's about 8 minutes, and it's a time. A light-year is a distance.

hints: Despite having 'year' in its name, it measures how far, not how long.
solution: A light-year is the **distance light travels in one year**, about 9.5 trillion km. It is used for the huge distances to stars.

prompt: The maramataka is the Māori calendar. It is based mainly on the phases of what?
hints: Its shape seems to change over about 29.5 days.
solution: The **Moon**. Each night of the Moon's cycle has its own name in the maramataka, and it is used with other signs in nature to plan activities such as planting, harvesting and fishing.

prompt: The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. What does this tell us about the seasons?

options.text: Distance can't be the cause of the seasons, because January is winter in the Northern Hemisphere
Distance causes the seasons, because January is summer in New Zealand
The whole Earth has summer in January
The seasons are caused by the Moon, not the Sun

feedback.b: If distance caused the seasons, the Northern Hemisphere would also have summer in January, but it has winter.
feedback.c: The two hemispheres always have opposite seasons.
feedback.d: The Moon doesn't cause seasons. The tilt of Earth's axis does.

hints: What season is it in Europe and North America in January?
solution: In January the Earth is closest to the Sun, yet the Northern Hemisphere has **winter**. So distance can't explain the seasons. The real cause is the **tilt** of Earth's axis.

prompt: A **solar** eclipse can only happen at which phase of the Moon?

options.text: New moon
Full moon
First quarter
Any phase

feedback.b: At full moon the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. That's when a lunar eclipse can happen.
feedback.c: At first quarter the Moon is to one side of the Sun–Earth line, so it can't block the Sun.
feedback.d: The Moon must be exactly between the Sun and the Earth, which only happens at one phase.

hints: In a solar eclipse, the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth.
solution: In a solar eclipse the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth. That only happens at **new moon**, when the Moon's lit side faces away from us.

prompt: Put the phases of the Moon in order, starting from **new moon**.
hints: Waxing (growing) phases come before full moon; waning (shrinking) phases come after.
Crescent is less than half lit; gibbous is more than half lit.
solution: New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent → back to new (about 29.5 days in total).

prompt: Mars is about 1.5 AU from the Sun, and 1 AU is about 150 million km. About how far is Mars from the Sun, in **millions of kilometres**?
hints: Multiply the distance in AU by the number of kilometres in 1 AU.
solution: $1.5 \times 150 = 225$, so Mars is about **225 million km** from the Sun.

prompt: Which statement about Matariki is accurate?

options.text: It is a cluster of stars (the Pleiades) whose rising before dawn in midwinter marks the Māori New Year for many iwi
It is a single bright planet that can be seen every night of the year
It is first seen in the evening sky in the middle of summer
It can only be seen from the Northern Hemisphere

feedback.b: Matariki is a cluster of many stars, not a planet, and for about a month each year it can't be seen at all.
feedback.c: Its important rising happens in the pre-dawn sky in midwinter (late June or July).
feedback.d: Matariki is easily seen from Aotearoa.

hints: When is the Matariki public holiday?
solution: Matariki is a **star cluster**, also called the Pleiades. After being hidden for about a month, it reappears low in the north-eastern sky **just before dawn in midwinter**, marking the Māori New Year for many iwi. Some iwi use the rising of Puanga (Rigel) instead.

prompt: Explain why the Moon appears to change shape (go through phases) during a month.
modelAnswer: The Moon doesn't make its own light. It reflects light from the Sun, and half of it is always lit. As the Moon orbits the Earth over about a month, we see different amounts of the lit half from Earth. At new moon we can't see the lit side at all, and at full moon we see all of it.

rubric.criterion: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun (the Moon reflects sunlight)
As the Moon orbits the Earth, we see different amounts of the lit half

hints: Does the Moon make its own light?
What changes during the month: the Moon's lit half, or our view of it?
solution: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As the Moon travels around the Earth, our view of that lit half changes, from none (new moon) to all of it (full moon) and back again.

prompt: Alpha Centauri, one of the Pointers next to the Southern Cross, is about 4.4 light-years away. When you look at it tonight, when did the light reaching your eyes leave the star?

options.text: About 4.4 years ago
About 4.4 days ago
At the same moment you see it
About 8 minutes ago

feedback.b: Light takes a whole year to travel one light-year.
feedback.c: Light is fast, but not instant. Over huge distances it takes a long time.
feedback.d: 8 minutes is how long light takes to reach us from the Sun, not from other stars.

hints: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year.
solution: Light takes one year to travel one light-year, so light from 4.4 light-years away left the star **about 4.4 years ago**. Looking at stars means looking back in time.

prompt: Explain why New Zealand is warmer in December than in June.
modelAnswer: Earth's axis is tilted (by about 23.5°), and it stays pointing the same way as the Earth orbits the Sun. In December the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun. The Sun is higher in the sky, so its light strikes the ground more directly and its energy is concentrated on a smaller area. Days are also longer, so there are more hours of heating. In June the Southern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, so the Sun is low, its light is spread out, and days are short. (It is not because the Earth is closer to the Sun; it is actually closest in January.)

rubric.criterion: Earth's axis is tilted and stays pointing the same way as the Earth orbits the Sun
In December the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so the Sun is higher and its light is more direct or concentrated
Days are longer in December, giving more hours of heating (or the reverse for June)

hints: Which way is the Southern Hemisphere tilted in December?
Think about how high the Sun gets and how long the days are.
solution: The tilt of the axis means that in December the Southern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun: the Sun is higher (more concentrated light) and days are longer, so it is summer. In June we lean away, which gives winter.

prompt: Mercury is closer to the Sun than Venus, but Venus is the hottest planet. Why?

options.text: Venus has a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat (a very strong greenhouse effect)
Venus is bigger, so it collects more sunlight
Venus spins faster, which heats it up
Mercury reflects all of its sunlight away

feedback.b: Venus is about Earth's size, and size isn't the reason. Earth is a similar size and much cooler.
feedback.c: Venus actually spins very slowly. One Venus day is longer than its year.
feedback.d: Mercury absorbs plenty of sunlight. It gets very hot by day but loses the heat at night, because it has no real atmosphere.

hints: Compare the atmospheres of Mercury and Venus.
solution: Venus has a very thick atmosphere of **carbon dioxide**, which traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect. Its surface is over 450 °C. Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so heat escapes and its night side gets very cold.

prompt: Light travels at about 300,000 km per second. The Sun is about 150,000,000 km from the Earth. How many seconds does sunlight take to reach the Earth?
hints: time = distance ÷ speed
solution: time = distance ÷ speed $= 150{,}000{,}000 \div 300{,}000 = $ **500 s**. That's 8 minutes 20 seconds. We always see the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago.

prompt: A few evenings after a new moon, a thin **waxing** crescent Moon is seen from New Zealand. Which side of the Moon is lit?

options.text: The left side
The right side
The top

feedback.b: That's how a waxing Moon looks from the Northern Hemisphere. From New Zealand the view is flipped.
feedback.c: The lit side always faces towards the Sun, which has just set in the west.

hints: The lit side always faces the Sun. After sunset, the Sun is below the western horizon.
From New Zealand we look north to see the Moon. When you face north, which side is west?
solution: The lit side faces the Sun, which has just set in the **west**. From New Zealand we look north to see the Moon, and west is on our **left**. So a waxing Moon is lit on the left, the opposite of what people in the Northern Hemisphere see.

prompt: Select **all** the statements that are true.

options.text: Mars has a thin atmosphere, mostly carbon dioxide
Venus is hotter than Mercury, even though it is further from the Sun
The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so its temperature changes hugely between day and night
Jupiter has a solid, rocky surface you could stand on
Saturn is closer to the Sun than Jupiter
Neptune is the closest planet to the Sun

hints: Jupiter is a gas giant.
Use the planet order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
solution: True: **Mars** has a thin CO₂ atmosphere; **Venus** is hotter than Mercury because of its greenhouse atmosphere; the **Moon** has almost no atmosphere to hold heat. False: Jupiter is a gas giant with no solid surface to stand on; Saturn is further out than Jupiter; Neptune is the furthest planet, not the closest.

prompt: The Moon goes around the Earth about once a month. Why don't we see a solar eclipse every month?

options.text: The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5°, so the Sun, Earth and Moon usually don't line up exactly
The Moon is too small to cast a shadow most months
Eclipses can only happen in summer
Clouds hide most eclipses

feedback.b: The Moon always casts a shadow. The shadow usually misses the Earth, passing above or below it.
feedback.c: Eclipses can happen at any time of year, whenever the Sun, Earth and Moon line up.
feedback.d: Clouds can block the view from one place, but the eclipse still happens.

hints: For an eclipse, the Sun, Earth and Moon must be in an exact straight line.
solution: The Moon's orbit is **tilted** about 5° compared with Earth's orbit around the Sun. Most months, at new moon, the Moon passes just above or below the Sun–Earth line, so its shadow misses the Earth. An eclipse happens only when new moon falls where the two orbits cross.

prompt: The Sun's diameter is about 400 times the Moon's diameter. Explain how the much smaller Moon can still completely cover the Sun during a total solar eclipse.
modelAnswer: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, but it is also about 400 times further away from the Earth. Because the extra distance makes the Sun look smaller by about the same amount, the Sun and Moon look almost exactly the same size in our sky. So when the Moon passes directly in front of the Sun, it can just cover it.

rubric.criterion: The Sun is much bigger (about 400 times wider) than the Moon
But the Sun is also much further away (about 400 times further)
So the Sun and Moon appear about the same size in the sky, and the Moon can just cover the Sun

hints: Hold a coin at arm's length and it can block out something much bigger that is far away.
Compare how far away the Sun and the Moon are.
solution: Size and distance cancel out: the Sun is about 400 times wider but also about 400 times further away, so the Sun and Moon look the same size, and the Moon can exactly cover the Sun.

prompt: Neptune is about 30 AU from the Sun. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to travel 1 AU. About how many **hours** does sunlight take to reach Neptune?
hints: First find the time in minutes for 30 AU.
There are 60 minutes in an hour.
solution: $30 \times 8 = 240$ minutes, and $240 \div 60 = $ **4 hours**. Out at Neptune, the Sun looks like a very bright star, and its light is much weaker.

prompt: Sketch C (13 November) shows a [[a]] Moon. Sketch E (20 November) shows a [[b]] Moon.
hints: "Gibbous" means more than half lit; "crescent" means less than half.
Waxing comes before the full moon (D); waning comes after it.
solution: C is more than half lit and comes before the full moon, so it is a **waxing gibbous** Moon. E is more than half lit and comes after the full moon, so it is a **waning gibbous** Moon.

prompt: The full moon was on 16 November. About how many days later will the next full moon be?
hints: How long does the Moon take to go through a whole cycle of phases?
solution: A full cycle of phases takes about **29.5 days**, so the next full moon will be about 29 or 30 days later, around 15 or 16 December.

prompt: A total lunar eclipse was seen from New Zealand on one of these six dates. Which date was it, and why could it only have happened then?
modelAnswer: It must have been 16 November, when the Moon was full (sketch D). A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth is directly between the Sun and the Moon, so the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. The Earth is only between the Sun and the Moon at full moon.

rubric.criterion: Chooses 16 November (full moon, sketch D)
A lunar eclipse needs the Earth between the Sun and the Moon, so the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, which only happens at full moon

hints: In a lunar eclipse, whose shadow falls on what?
Where is the Moon compared with the Sun and the Earth at full moon?
solution: **16 November** (full moon). Only at full moon is the Earth between the Sun and the Moon, so its shadow can fall on the Moon.

options.text: Position A
Position B
Both positions
Neither position

feedback.c: The seasons are opposite at A and B, because the hemisphere leaning towards the Sun changes.
feedback.d: At one of these positions the Southern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun, which gives New Zealand summer.

hints: New Zealand is in the Southern Hemisphere.
At which position does the South Pole lean towards the Sun?
solution: At **position B** the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so it is summer in New Zealand (December). At A it is New Zealand's winter (June).

prompt: Suppose the Earth's axis were **not tilted at all**. What would happen to the seasons?

options.text: There would be almost no seasons: each place would get about the same sunlight all year
The seasons would be the same as now, because they are caused by the distance from the Sun
Both hemispheres would have summer all year round
There would be no day and night

feedback.b: Earth's distance from the Sun changes only a little during the year. The tilt is what causes the seasons.
feedback.c: Without a tilt, neither hemisphere would ever lean towards the Sun, so there would be no summer or winter.
feedback.d: Day and night come from the Earth spinning on its axis, which would still happen without a tilt.

hints: What causes the seasons now?
solution: The seasons are caused by the **tilt**. Without it, the Sun would reach the same height at midday and days would be the same length all year at any place, so there would be almost no seasons. Day and night would carry on, because the Earth would still spin.

The table shows some data about five planets.

| Planet | Average distance from the Sun (AU) | Time to orbit the Sun | Average surface temperature (°C) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mercury | 0.39 | 88 days | 167 |
| Venus | 0.72 | 225 days | 464 |
| Earth | 1.0 | 365 days | 15 |
| Mars | 1.5 | 687 days | −65 |
| Jupiter | 5.2 | 12 years | −110 (top of the clouds) |
prompt: Which pattern does the data show?

options.text: The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer it takes to orbit the Sun
The closer a planet is to the Sun, the longer it takes to orbit the Sun
All the planets take the same time to orbit the Sun
There is no link between distance and the time to orbit

feedback.b: Check the table: Mercury, the closest, takes only 88 days, while Jupiter takes 12 years.
feedback.c: The times range from 88 days to 12 years.
feedback.d: As the distance increases down the table, the orbit time increases every time.

hints: Compare the distance column with the orbit time column, row by row.
solution: The **further** a planet is from the Sun, the **longer** it takes to orbit: it has further to travel and it moves more slowly.

|---|---|---|---|
| Mercury | 0.39 | 88 days | 167 |
| Venus | 0.72 | 225 days | 464 |
| Earth | 1.0 | 365 days | 15 |
| Mars | 1.5 | 687 days | −65 |
| Jupiter | 5.2 | 12 years | −110 (top of the clouds) |
prompt: Use the data to help explain why Earth is the only planet in the table that has liquid water on its surface.
modelAnswer: Water is liquid between 0 °C and 100 °C. Earth's average temperature is 15 °C, which is in this range, so water can stay liquid. Mercury (167 °C) and Venus (464 °C) are far too hot: any water would boil away. Mars (−65 °C) is too cold, so its water is frozen, and its thin atmosphere means liquid water would not last. Jupiter is a gas giant with no solid surface for water to sit on, and it is extremely cold.

rubric.criterion: Earth's average temperature (15 °C) is between 0 °C and 100 °C, so water can be liquid
Mercury and Venus are too hot (water would boil or evaporate away)
Mars is too cold (water freezes) and/or Jupiter has no solid surface and is very cold

hints: Between which temperatures is water a liquid?
Compare each planet's temperature with that range.
solution: Only Earth's temperature is between 0 and 100 °C. Mercury and Venus are too hot, Mars is too cold, and Jupiter is a cold gas giant with no surface.

prompt: Why can we see the Moon in the night sky?

options.text: It reflects light from the Sun
It makes its own light, like a star
It is very hot and glows
It reflects light from cities on Earth

feedback.b: The Moon is not a star. It gives out no light of its own.
feedback.c: The Moon is a cold, rocky object at night. It does not glow from heat.
feedback.d: City lights are far too faint. The Moon is lit by the Sun.

hints: The Moon is a rocky object, not a star.
solution: The Moon **reflects sunlight**. We only see the part of it that is lit by the Sun, which is why it seems to change shape.

prompt: Which is the largest planet in our Solar System?
hints: It is a gas giant, the fifth planet from the Sun.
solution: **Jupiter** is the largest planet. More than 1000 Earths could fit inside it.

prompt: In which direction does the Sun rise?

options.text: East
West
North
South

feedback.b: The Sun sets in the west.
feedback.c: In New Zealand the Sun is in the northern part of the sky at midday, but it rises in the east.
feedback.d: From New Zealand the Sun never appears in the south at midday, and it rises in the east.

hints: The Earth spins towards the east.
solution: The Sun rises in the **east** and sets in the west, because the Earth spins from west to east.

prompt: At midday in New Zealand, where is the Sun in the sky?

options.text: In the northern part of the sky
Directly overhead
In the southern part of the sky
Low down in the east

feedback.b: The Sun is only ever directly overhead in the tropics. New Zealand is too far south.
feedback.c: That is true in places such as the United Kingdom, in the Northern Hemisphere. New Zealand is in the Southern Hemisphere.
feedback.d: The Sun is low in the east in the early morning, not at midday.

hints: New Zealand is well south of the tropics, so the Sun never passes directly overhead.
solution: From New Zealand, the midday Sun is always in the **northern** part of the sky. That is why north-facing windows and gardens get the most sun here.

prompt: Select **all** the **rocky** planets.

options.text: Mercury
Venus
Earth
Mars
Jupiter
Saturn
Uranus
Neptune

hints: The rocky planets are the four closest to the Sun.
solution: **Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars** are small, rocky planets. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, and Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. None of the outer four has a solid surface you could stand on.

prompt: The star cluster Matariki can't be seen in May, but it reappears in the eastern sky just before dawn in midwinter (June or July). Why can't it be seen in May?

options.text: In May, Matariki is in the same direction as the Sun, so it is lost in the Sun's glare
Matariki orbits the Sun, and in May it is behind the Sun
The stars of Matariki stop shining for part of each year
Matariki can only be seen in cold weather

feedback.b: Matariki is a cluster of stars hundreds of light-years away. It does not orbit the Sun. It is the Earth that moves.
feedback.c: The stars shine all the time. We just can't see them in daylight.
feedback.d: Temperature doesn't decide whether we can see stars. Their direction compared with the Sun does.

hints: Can you see stars in the daytime sky?
As the Earth orbits the Sun, the Sun appears in front of different groups of stars.
solution: As the Earth orbits the Sun, the Sun lines up with different stars during the year. In May, Matariki is in the **same direction as the Sun**, so it is up in the daytime and hidden by sunlight. As the Earth moves on, Matariki rises earlier each day until it can be seen just before dawn in midwinter.

prompt: Since 2022, Matariki has been a public holiday in Aotearoa New Zealand. Why is the holiday on a different date each year?

options.text: Its date is set using the maramataka, which follows the phases of the Moon rather than fixed calendar dates
The date is chosen at random each year
Matariki moves to a different part of the sky each year
It is always on the shortest day of the year, and the shortest day moves by several weeks

feedback.b: The date is not random. It is worked out in advance from the maramataka.
feedback.c: Matariki rises in the same part of the sky at about the same time each year.
feedback.d: The shortest day is always around 21 June. The holiday moves because it follows the Moon.

hints: The maramataka is a lunar calendar. Do Moon phases fall on the same dates each year?
solution: The date follows the **maramataka**, the Māori lunar calendar. Moon phases fall on different dates each year in our usual calendar, so the holiday falls on a different Friday in June or July each year.

prompt: Put these in order of distance from the Earth, from **closest** to **furthest**.
hints: The Sun is the closest star. Neptune is in our Solar System.
Light from Alpha Centauri takes about 4 years to reach us; light from Matariki takes hundreds of years.
solution: Moon (about 384,000 km) → Sun (about 150 million km) → Neptune (about 30 times further than the Sun) → Alpha Centauri (about 4.4 light-years) → Matariki (about 440 light-years).

prompt: Light travels at about 300,000 km per second. The Moon is about 384,000 km from the Earth. How many seconds does light from the Moon take to reach us? Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
hints: time = distance ÷ speed
solution: time = 384,000 ÷ 300,000 = 1.28 s ≈ **1.3 s**. So we see the Moon as it was just over a second ago.

prompt: To find south using the Southern Cross, imagine a line along the [[a]] axis of the Cross. Extend this line about [[b]] times its own length. The point you reach is roughly above due south.
hints: The Cross has a longer arm and a shorter arm. The longer one points towards the south celestial pole.
solution: Extend the **long** axis of the Southern Cross about **4.5** times its length. Then drop straight down to the horizon to find south. Stars like these have long helped people find their way at night.

prompt: From Earth, we always see the same side of the Moon. Why?

options.text: The Moon spins once on its axis in the same time it takes to orbit the Earth once
The Moon does not spin at all
The other side of the Moon is always dark, so we can't see it
The Earth's shadow always covers the other side of the Moon

feedback.b: If the Moon didn't spin, we would see all sides of it as it travelled around the Earth.
feedback.c: The far side gets sunlight too. At new moon the far side is fully lit.
feedback.d: The Earth's shadow only falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse.

hints: Try walking around a chair while always facing it. How many times do you turn around?
solution: The Moon spins once on its axis in about 27 days, the **same time** it takes to orbit the Earth. So the same side always faces us. The far side is not always dark; we just never see it from Earth.

prompt: During a total lunar eclipse, the Moon usually looks a dark reddish colour instead of disappearing completely. Why?

options.text: Some sunlight is bent through Earth's atmosphere onto the Moon, and mostly red light gets through
The Moon heats up in the Earth's shadow and glows red
Mars shines red light onto the Moon
The Moon gives out its own red light when sunlight is blocked

feedback.b: In the Earth's shadow the Moon cools down, not heats up.
feedback.c: Mars reflects sunlight too, but far too little to light up the Moon.
feedback.d: The Moon has no light of its own. Any light on it comes from the Sun.

hints: Sunrises and sunsets look red for a related reason.
solution: Earth's atmosphere **bends (refracts)** some sunlight into the shadow. On its long path through the air, most of the blue light is scattered away, so mostly **red** light reaches the Moon. It is like all the world's sunrises and sunsets lighting up the Moon at once.

prompt: Long before compasses were used, navigators on voyaging waka crossed the Pacific Ocean. Describe how stars can be used to keep a direction when travelling at sea at night.
modelAnswer: Because the Earth spins, stars rise in the east, move across the sky and set in the west. Each star always rises and sets at the same point on the horizon. Navigators memorised where many particular stars rise and set. To travel in a chosen direction, they steered towards a star that was low on the horizon in that direction. When that star rose too high to be useful, they changed to the next star that rose at the same point, so a series of stars through the night kept them on course. They combined this with other signs, such as the direction of the ocean swells, the winds and the flight of seabirds.

rubric.criterion: Stars rise and set at fixed points on the horizon (they move across the sky because the Earth spins)
Navigators memorised where particular stars rise or set, and steered towards a star low on the horizon in the direction they wanted
Used a series of stars rising at the same point through the night, or combined stars with other signs such as swells, winds or birds

hints: Does a star always rise at the same place on the horizon?
What could a navigator do once their guide star had risen high in the sky?
solution: Stars rise and set at fixed points on the horizon. Steering towards a series of known stars rising (or setting) in the wanted direction keeps a course, checked against swells, winds and birds.

prompt: The Moon's surface can be over 100 °C in the daytime and below −130 °C at night, but the Earth's temperature changes much less between day and night. Explain why.
modelAnswer: The Moon has almost no atmosphere. Without air to trap heat (no greenhouse effect) and spread it around, the sunlit surface heats up strongly, and at night the heat escapes straight into space, so the surface gets extremely cold. The Moon also spins slowly: one day–night cycle takes about a month, so each part of the surface is in sunlight for about two weeks and then in darkness for about two weeks, giving it a long time to heat up and cool down. Earth has a thick atmosphere that traps heat at night and spreads heat around, and it spins once every 24 hours, so day and night temperatures stay much closer together.

rubric.criterion: The Moon has (almost) no atmosphere, whereas Earth has a thick atmosphere
Without an atmosphere, heat is not trapped or spread around, so it escapes into space at night and the day side heats strongly
The Moon's day and night each last about two weeks (it spins slowly), giving long times to heat up and cool down; Earth spins every 24 hours

hints: What does Earth's atmosphere do at night?
How long does daytime last at one place on the Moon?
solution: No atmosphere on the Moon to trap and spread heat, plus two-week-long days and nights, give huge temperature swings. Earth's atmosphere and 24-hour spin keep them small.

prompt: A total **solar** eclipse can only be seen from a narrow strip of the Earth's surface. A total **lunar** eclipse can be seen from anywhere on the night side of the Earth. Explain why.
modelAnswer: In a solar eclipse, the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth. The Moon is much smaller than the Earth, so the darkest part of its shadow covers only a small area, which moves across the Earth as a narrow strip. Only people in that strip see the Sun completely covered. In a lunar eclipse, the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. The Earth's shadow is much bigger than the Moon, so it can cover the whole Moon, and everyone who can see the Moon at that time, which is everyone on the night side of the Earth, sees it darkened.

rubric.criterion: Solar eclipse: the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth, and because the Moon is small its dark shadow covers only a small area (narrow strip)
Lunar eclipse: the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon and is big enough to cover the whole Moon
So everyone who can see the Moon (the whole night side) sees the lunar eclipse

hints: In each type of eclipse, whose shadow falls on what?
Compare the size of the Moon's shadow with the size of the Earth.
solution: Solar: the small Moon casts a small shadow on the big Earth (narrow strip). Lunar: the big Earth's shadow covers the whole Moon, visible to everyone who can see the Moon.

prompt: In a scale model of the Solar System, 1 m represents 1 million km. Neptune is about 30 AU from the Sun, and 1 AU is about 150 million km. How far from the model Sun should the model Neptune be? Give your answer in **kilometres**.
hints: First find Neptune's real distance in millions of kilometres.
Each million kilometres becomes 1 m in the model. Then convert metres to kilometres.
solution: Real distance = 30 × 150 million km = 4500 million km. In the model that is 4500 m = **4.5 km**. (On the same scale the Sun would be a ball only about 1.4 m across.)
